title: The water carrier
hookLine: for years he carries water for Guru Angad before dawn; tradition says he stumbled by a weaver's peg and was mocked as homeless

lines: TO THE RIVER AND BACK, BEFORE DAWN.
THE SAME SMALL JOB, FOR YEARS.
cards: Every morning, long before sunrise, Amar Das, the old man who'd come to Khadur, walked to the river Beas, filled a pitcher with water, and carried it back for Guru Angad's bath.
A long walk, there and back, in the dark, every day, in every season. Tradition says he did it for twelve years.

It's the kind of job some people do faithfully for years: the crossing guard there every morning in the rain, the neighbor who's brought in your trash cans since you moved in, the parent who packs the lunch every school day.
Nobody writes songs about them. Today, one stormy night on that road.

teach.h: A WEAVER'S PEG, IN THE RAIN.
teach.b: It was dark and pouring rain, tradition says, and the old man was coming back with the full pitcher.
Near a weaver's house he tripped over a peg in the ground, one of the stakes weavers use to stretch their thread, and fell. He didn't spill the water.
But the noise woke the weaver, who asked who was out there at that hour.

His wife answered, scornfully: it must be Amru, the homeless one, who has no place of his own and hangs around the Guru for scraps. Amar Das didn't argue. He picked himself up and carried the water home.
When the story reached Guru Angad, tradition says, he answered with a list of honors: Amar Das is the home of the homeless, the honor of those with no honor, the strength of those with none.
Not long after, he named Amar Das the third Guru. Sikhs keep telling this because it turns the insult inside out. The one mocked as having no place becomes the one who gives everyone a place.
Now look back at the week. The sheet of flowers, for everyone. Lehna becomes Angad, part of the Guru's own body.
The Guru's script, letters for everyone. Mata Khivi's kitchen. The wrestling ground.
An old man who heard a hymn. And a water carrier on a dark road. Again and again, people were chosen, or remembered, for faithfulness when nobody was watching.
Guru Angad's light passed to the man who carried the water.

how: Sikhs honor Guru Amar Das's years of carrying water as a model of seva, humble service; Guru Angad's reply to the weaver's wife is often recited in the story, and Sikhs often volunteer in small, unseen tasks at the gurdwara.

games.q: you're an old man who's just fallen in the mud in the dark, and a stranger calls you a homeless hanger-on. what do you do?
o: argue and explain who you are.
pick yourself up and carry the water home.
give up the job; it's not worth it.
games.why: Amar Das said nothing and carried the water home. Guru Angad called him the home of the homeless, and soon named him Guru.

practice: Think of one small thing you do for someone that nobody notices: filling the water jug, taking out the recycling, checking on an elderly neighbor.
Picture doing it a little more carefully than usual, without mentioning it to anyone. If someone mocks it, or ignores it, let it go; just carry the water.

wordCard.voice: Seva. Selfless service, the heart of the years Amar Das spent carrying water before dawn for Guru Angad, mocked as homeless, and named the home of the homeless.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: seva, selfless service; the heart of the water carrier's years.
